title: Canada blasts Iran for closing Kazemi trial
article: The federal government accused Iranian officials of contradicting each other yesterday about why Canadians have been barred from the trial of the man accused of killing Zahra Kazemi, saying the account of Iran's ambassador conflicts with that of its Foreign Minister.

Sources close to Canadian Foreign Affairs Minister Bill Graham flatly rejected assertions by the Iranian ambassador yesterday that a judge, not the government, issued the order to keep foreign observers out of the court.
"Never was the premise raised that it was a decision of the judiciary," a source close to Mr. Graham said. "This is a completely new argument."
Ms. Kazemi, a 54-year-old photojournalist, died of a fractured skull, the result of a beating after she was arrested for taking photographs outside a Tehran prison.

An angry Mr. Graham called back Canada's ambassador to Iran on Wednesday to protest against the decision to bar observers. He has suggested Canada may try to take Iran to the World Court or, perhaps, impose economic sanctions.
Mr. Graham also issued strenuous objections on Wednesday to Iranian Ambassador Mohammad Mousavi.

After the meeting with Mr. Graham, Mr. Mousavi gave several interviews to deflect suggestions that the Iranian government was responsible for reneging on the pledge to allow Canadian observers, saying instead that the responsibility rested with one judge.
But the federal source said yesterday that Iran's government made the decision.

The source said the country's Foreign Minister, Kamal Kharrazi, indicated to Mr. Graham in a personal telephone call on June 24 that the government intended to reverse its stand on allowing observers.

Mr. Kharrazi told Mr. Graham that the reason for the reversal was ostensibly the shooting of an Iranian student in Canada. The student, 18-year-old Keyvan Tabesh, was killed by a police officer in the Vancouver suburb of Port Moody after wielding a machete. That incident will be the subject of an inquest.

"On June 24, Mr. Kharrazi, making a direct link with the situation with Tabesh, clearly used accusing comments about the way Canada handled the Tabesh case," said the source. "\[He said\] under the circumstances, it would not be possible for observers. That comes from the mouth of the Foreign Minister."

Canadian officials are concerned that a low-level intelligence officer will be convicted in Ms. Kazemi's death when responsibility may more appropriately lie with senior officials of the Iranian government.
Canadian officials say lack of Canadian representation will undermine the trial's credibility.
Yesterday, John Terry, the lawyer for Ms. Kazemi's son, Stephan Hachemi, said he is pressing hard for federal officials to take Iran to the International Court of Justice.
Mr. Terry said Ottawa has advised Mr. Hachemi to ensure a lawyer represents him in the Iranian court, to keep the doors open for further action at the World Court.
Mr. Hachemi will be represented in Iran by a team led by Shirin Ebadi, a Nobel Peace Prize laureate and human-rights lawyer.
Mr. Terry also rejected suggestions by the Iranian ambassador that a judge ruled against allowing Canadian monitors.
"The decision to bar foreigners from a trial is going to be made at the level of the Ministry of Justice," Mr. Terry said. "It's not just something that a judge on their own would do."
